explanations.explanation: That's the word Paul uses: the strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak. Bearing with someone means you stay close and carry it with them. And notice he says "we," so he counts himself in with the strong. I've bent a few stamps in my day, so I know how good it feels when somebody is patient with me.

Paul never says that. He says to bear with the shortcomings, not to announce them. Pointing out a shortcoming is like holding up a cookie with a chipped edge and calling the whole room over to see it. Paul's word is "bear with," and it comes right before “…and not to please ourselves.”

Paul doesn't give us that option. To bear with someone you have to stay near enough to carry something with them. Keeping your distance is easier, I'll admit it, but that isn't what verse 1 says. He says the strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak.

Paul says the opposite. The verse says the strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak “…and not to please ourselves.” So the strong don't get to put themselves first. The whole verse points the other way, toward carrying the weak.

Right, because Paul says the strong ought to bear with the shortcomings of the weak “…and not to please ourselves.” Pleasing ourselves first is the thing he steers us away from. He points the strong toward the weak instead. Nobody gets to be first in line at the cooling rack on this one.

Paul says to please your neighbor for his good, “…to build him up.” So the goal isn't just making somebody smile for a minute. It's helping him grow stronger. Building up is slow work, friend, like stacking a tall cookie box without crushing the bottom row.

Paul doesn't say that. Winning someone over is about getting your way, and Paul just told us not to please ourselves. What he says is to please your neighbor for his good, to build him up. The aim is his good, not your win.

That's not in the verse. Paul says to please your neighbor for his good, to build him up. Hushing somebody doesn't build anybody up, it just makes the room quieter. Building up is about helping him stand taller.

Paul quotes the words “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.” (Psalm 69:9) He uses them to show that even Christ did not please Himself. I think that's a heavy line, and it's worth sitting with for a second. Jesus took that weight on Himself instead of putting Himself first.

The quote goes the other direction. What fell on Christ were insults, not honors. Paul's words are “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.” (Psalm 69:9) I think that's a heavy line, and it shows what it looked like for Christ not to please Himself.

No rewards in this one. Paul's quote says “The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.” (Psalm 69:9) That's Paul's example of Christ not pleasing Himself. I think it's a heavy line, so it's worth slowing down for.

Paul says everything written in the past was written for our instruction. So those old words are there to teach us. I read a recipe so I can bake the thing, not so I can frame the page. Paul goes on to say it gives us endurance, encouragement and hope.

Paul's word here is instruction, not judgment. He says everything written in the past was written for our instruction. Then he says why: that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope. It's meant to teach us and give us hope.

The old writings are old, so I get why history comes to mind. But Paul's word is instruction. He says everything written in the past was written for our instruction. They're there to teach us, so that we might have hope.

That's the word. Paul asks God to grant harmony so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify “…the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” One mind and one voice, friend, and not a single person sneaking in a different song. The harmony points to God.

Obeying is a good thing, but it isn't Paul's word here. He says that with one mind and one voice you may glorify “…the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The harmony is there so they can give God glory together.

Seeking God is a fine thing to do, but Paul says something else in this verse. The harmony is so that with one mind and one voice you may glorify “…the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Glorify is the word Paul uses. They do it together, with one voice.

Paul says to accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you. Christ is the measuring stick, and Paul doesn't put himself up there. Honestly, I'd be nervous if my name were the standard. I can't even stamp a straight line some days.

Paul is the one writing the letter, but he points past himself. He says to accept one another just as Christ accepted you. He doesn't make himself the example. I like a writer who hands the spotlight to somebody better.
Moses, Israel's leader, doesn't show up in this verse. Paul says to accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you. Christ is the example Paul points to. That's the whole picture.
Paul says accepting one another is “…in order to bring glory to God.” So it isn't only about getting along. It brings glory to God. He ties it back to Christ, who accepted you.
Paul says the opposite. He says to accept one another, just as Christ accepted you, “…in order to bring glory to God.” So accepting each other does bring glory to God. That's the point he's making.

Paul says Christ became a servant “…so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy.” The Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. Mercy is what this part is about. Paul wants them praising God for it.

Priests don't come up here. Paul says Christ became a servant to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, “…so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy.” The Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. They're the ones Paul names.
No angels in this verse. Paul says it's “…so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy.” The Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. Paul is talking about people, and they're the ones he names.

The quote says “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.” So the Gentiles aren't rejoicing off in a corner by themselves. They're rejoicing together with God's people. Paul is showing both groups in one celebration.
Kings aren't in this quote. It says “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.” The Gentiles are told to rejoice with God's people. It's a rejoicing together, and nobody is told to wait on a king.
The prophets aren't named in this one. The quote says “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people.” The Gentiles are invited to rejoice with God's people. That's what Paul is lining up.

This one doesn't say "some." It says “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.” All the Gentiles and all the peoples are told to praise. I checked it twice, and "all" doesn't leave anybody out.

Right, because the quote says “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and extol Him, all you peoples.” It's all the Gentiles and all the peoples, not only some. When a verse says all twice in one breath, I don't go hunting for exceptions.
Isaiah's words are “…in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.” Their hope rests in Him, the Root of Jesse. That's what Paul has been building toward: the Gentiles have a real place to put their hope.

That's a nice picture, but it's not what Isaiah says. The words are “…in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.” It's about hope, not a home. I know a thing or two about wanting a better address, but Paul's word here is hope.
Keeping the law isn't in Isaiah's words here. They say “…in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.” What the Gentiles do is put their hope in Him.

Paul says you may overflow with hope “…by the power of the Holy Spirit.” The hope doesn't come from trying harder. It overflows by the Spirit's power. And friend, overflow is the word, like a cookie jar nobody can close.
Paul himself is an apostle (Romans 1:1), but he doesn't point to the apostles here. He says you may overflow with hope “…by the power of the Holy Spirit.” That's where the power comes from.
Elders aren't named in this verse. Paul says you may overflow with hope “…by the power of the Holy Spirit.” The Holy Spirit is the power behind the overflow. Paul doesn't credit anybody else.
